title: The stall is not a problem
summary: When a brisket or shoulder parks at 160°F for hours, the meat is evaporating, not failing. Wrap for time. Wait for bark.

body.text: Every all-day cook hits a wall somewhere between 150 and 170°F internal. This is evaporative cooling — the same physics as sweat.

body.heading: Wrap for the clock, not for fear
body.text: Butcher paper slows evaporation without turning bark to stew. Foil is faster and wetter. Neither is mandatory. If the bark is mahogany and dinner is flexible, ride the stall out.

body.heading: What the stall is not
body.text: It is not the fat rendering. It is not collagen magically converting at 160. Collagen starts dissolving closer to 180–200. The stall is weather on the surface.

takeaways: Expect 2–4 hours of stall on a packer or a butt.
Wrap only after bark is set, and only if you need the time.
Paper breathes; foil braises. Choose on purpose.

title: Bark is a crust you earn
summary: Bark is dried spice, rendered fat, smoke, and Maillard. If it rubs off, you never had it.

body.text: Good bark looks like mahogany leather. Wait until the rub has tacked on. If you wrap before the color is finished, you unwrap steamed spice, not bark.

takeaways: Set the bark before you wrap. Always.

title: Thin blue smoke or go home
summary: White billowing smoke is unburned wood. Learn to feed a fire so it always has flame.

body.text: Dirty smoke is a fire problem, not a wood problem. Small splits, often, with flame always visible.

takeaways: If you can see the smoke from the street, it is too thick.

title: Temperature is a rumor
summary: Brisket at 203°F is a guideline. Probe tender is the law.

body.text: Slide a probe into the flat. If it takes a shove, it is not done. If it slides like warm butter, pull it.

title: Resting is still cooking
summary: A brisket sliced the minute it hits temp is a dry brisket.

body.text: Hold unsliced in a dry cooler or a 150°F oven at least an hour, two to four if you can.

title: Match the wood to the animal
summary: Post oak for beef, hickory for pork, fruitwood for birds. Mesquite is a spice, not a 12-hour fuel.

body.text: A chunk of mesquite in a short steak cook is a gift. Twelve hours of it is a punishment.

title: Fat cap up, down, or does it matter?
summary: Heat source decides. The cap is a shield, not a baster of miracles.

body.text: On an offset, point the thick end at the firebox. Fat does not baste through meat like a cartoon.

takeaways: Trim to about a quarter inch.

title: Spritz, mop, or leave it alone
summary: Most cooks overdo liquid on meat.

body.text: After bark is set, a light mist every 45–60 minutes is enough. Leave it alone for the first 3–4 hours.

takeaways: Don't wash the crust into the pan.

title: Salt early, sugar late
summary: A dry brine is the cheapest upgrade in barbecue.

body.text: Salt overnight if you can. Put sugar in a late glaze, not a 14-hour crust.

title: What the circuit doesn't tell you
summary: Competition is a judged bite. Backyard is a table.

body.text: Steal clean fire, honest rest, and the nerve to wait on bark. Leave the syringe unless you like it.

takeaways: Backyard is a table, not a scorecard.
